explain.say: Power stations that burn fuel or split atoms are heat engines: they turn heat into motion. A heat engine only works while heat flows from something hot to something cold, and some heat must always reach the cold side.

faq.q: Why does a heat engine need a cold side?
faq.a: A heat engine makes work from heat flowing from hot to cold, like a water wheel needs water flowing downhill. If everything were the same temperature, no heat would flow and nothing would turn.
asks: Why do power stations need cooling?

faq.q: Why can't the steam heat be reused?
faq.a: The leftover steam is only about 30 to 40 degrees Celsius, far too cool to boil water for the turbine again. Its heat is plentiful but low grade, so it is only useful for gentle jobs like warming nearby buildings or greenhouses.
asks: Why not reuse the waste heat?

faq.q: What limits a power station's efficiency?
faq.a: The temperatures of the hot steam and the cold cooling water set an upper limit, called the Carnot efficiency. On top of that, friction, leaks and heat lost up the chimney take a further share.

faq.q: Why not make the steam even hotter?
faq.a: At very high temperature and pressure, steel slowly stretches and weakens over time. Special nickel alloys could allow steam at around 700 degrees Celsius, but they are very expensive.
asks: How hot can steam in a power station get?

faq.q: Do wind and solar farms waste heat too?
faq.a: Wind turbines and solar panels are not heat engines, so they do not need a cold side and have no Carnot limit. They still lose some energy in other ways, but there is no cooling water to dump heat into.

facts: The Carnot efficiency, the most any heat engine can achieve, is 1 minus the cold temperature divided by the hot temperature, both measured in kelvin.
Modern ultra-supercritical coal plants use steam at around 600 degrees Celsius and reach about 45 percent efficiency.
